story: This Hubble image shows the globular cluster 47 Tucanae, also called NGC 104, which belongs to the constellation Tucana, the Toucan, in the southern sky. It hosts tens of thousands of stars and is second only to Omega Centauri in brightness among the night sky's globular clusters.

Scientists used Hubble to study the cluster's white dwarfs, the faint remnants of dying stars. These stars move out from the crowded center of the cluster toward its outskirts. Astronomers already knew the process should happen, but it had never been seen in action until this detailed study of 47 Tucanae.

In crowded clusters, gravitational encounters between stars tend to sort them by mass over time, with heavier stars settling inward and lighter ones spreading outward. Watching white dwarfs travel outward gives a direct look at how a cluster rearranges its stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.80 x 2.74 arcminutes) and distance (15000 light years), the frame spans roughly 12 × 12 light-years. Its light set out about 15,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines ultraviolet light from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 with visible and near-infrared light from its Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared data lie beyond what the eye can see, and Hubble's sharp view separates the individual stars of this crowded cluster.
